stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 8.2 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 319 K and 0.98 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 27.0 mL of 0.14 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.12 M NaOH.
2.5 g of $$\ce{NH4NO3}$$ dissolves in 134 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 9.3 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Mg electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and a Cu electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Cu^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e- -> Mg}$$ E° = -2.37 V; $$\ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e- -> Cu}$$ E° = 0.34 V.
The photoelectron spectra of N (Z = 7) and O (Z = 8) are compared.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.002 M solution of $$\ce{HNO3}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] equals its concentration.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 6.4. In a solution at pH 5.5, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 55 g of $$\ce{CH4}$$?

options.why: Correct. n = m/M with M = 16.04 g/mol.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.002 M solution of $$\ce{Ba(OH)2}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Each formula unit releases two OH⁻.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.002 M; pH = 14 − pOH.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
That is the pOH; subtract from 14.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 7.1 g. The actual yield is 6.8 g. What is the percent yield?
A reaction has K = 15. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 338 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH negative, which change shifts the equilibrium toward NH₃?

options.why: The reaction is exothermic; heating shifts left.
Correct. The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.explanation: The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.stem: When a salt dissolves in water, the temperature of the solution decreases. Which is true?

options.text: The process is endothermic; energy flows from the water into the dissolving process
The water's molecules gain kinetic energy

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{CH4}$$, $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
CH4 has a larger molar mass (16 g/mol).
He has a larger molar mass (4 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: CH4 16, He 4, Ar 40, H2 2.02.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.2).

questions.stem: What volume does 1.1 mol of gas occupy at 1.57 atm and 348 K?

options.why: 22.4 L/mol applies only at 0 °C and 1 atm.
Use R = 0.08206 with atm and L.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of a sample of copper shows two peaks: mass 63 with relative abundance 26% and mass 65 with 74%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.
Pair each mass with its own abundance.
The isotopes are not equally abundant.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ is consumed at 0.15 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NH3}$$ form?

options.why: Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 2/3.
Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 9.5. A mixture has [A] = 0.1 M, [B] = 0.5 M and [C] = 0.4 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 8
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 3.2
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 3.2, which is less than K.

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 3.2
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 1.04 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 259 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.186 mol of solute in enough water to make 860 mL of solution?
50 mL of 0.28 M weak acid HA is titrated with 0.13 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH reaches the equivalence point?

options.why: Correct. Moles of base = moles of acid.

questions.stem: In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, [Zn²⁺] is increased. What happens to the cell potential?

options.why: Correct. A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.explanation: A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.stem: In paper chromatography with a nonpolar solvent, which component travels farthest?

options.why: Correct. It is most attracted to the nonpolar mobile phase.
Polar components stay with the polar paper.

questions.explanation: It is most attracted to the nonpolar mobile phase.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 18. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.8 mol N₂, 0.3 mol O₂ and 0.8 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1.1 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: Which Lewis structure is preferred when formal charges are considered?

options.text: The one with positive charge on the most electronegative atom
The one with the most double bonds
The one with the largest formal charges
The one with formal charges closest to zero and any negative charge on the most electronegative atom
options.why: Correct. That is the formal charge criterion.

questions.explanation: That is the formal charge criterion.

questions.stem: In a mechanism, a species that is produced in one step and consumed in a later step is a(n):

options.why: A catalyst is consumed first and regenerated later.
Correct. It does not appear in the overall equation.

questions.explanation: It does not appear in the overall equation.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{Ar}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: Ar 40, O2 32, H2 2.02, N2 28.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{CaO}$$ or $$\ce{NaF}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{CaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{NaF}$$, because its ions have larger charges
$$\ce{NaF}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

questions.explanation: CaO has ion charges 2 and 2; NaF has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: Which is a physical change?

options.why: Correct. Only intermolecular forces are overcome.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 27.5 g. The actual yield is 19.5 g. What is the percent yield?
139 g of water at 68 °C is mixed with 58 g of water at 23 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own temperature.
Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of O in $$\ce{H2SO4}$$?

options.why: There are 4 atoms of O in the formula.
That is the percent of the other elements.
Use masses, not numbers of atoms.

questions.stem: Which indicator is best for titrating acetic acid with NaOH (equivalence pH ≈ 8.7)?

options.why: Correct. Its range includes the equivalence pH.

questions.explanation: Its range includes the equivalence pH.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 749 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 117 kJ/mol, the transition state at 247 kJ/mol and the products at 4 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the forward reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 130, ΔH = -113, reverse Ea = 243 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{2N2O5 -> 4NO2 + O2}$$, $$\ce{N2O5}$$ is consumed at 0.77 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NO2}$$ form?

options.why: Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 4/2.
Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.

questions.stem: 22 mL of 4.8 M solution is diluted to 122 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + Br2 -> 2HBr}$$.

options.why: Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).

questions.stem: A 36.8 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 26.1 mL of 0.058 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 5 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 6. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{6}$$, which has 18 electrons.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{BaSO4}$$ is 1.1 \times 10^{-10}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?

options.why: This salt gives two ions: Ksp = s².

questions.stem: For the galvanic cell made from these half-cells, what is ΔG°? (F = 96,485 C/mol)

options.why: ΔG° is negative for a positive E°.
Correct. ΔG° = −nFE° with n = 2 electrons transferred and E° = 0.46 V.

questions.stem: What is the molecular geometry of $$\ce{NH3}$$?

options.why: Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Correct. Count electron domains and lone pairs on the central atom.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.173 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
Which substance is most soluble in hexane (C₆H₁₄)?

options.why: Ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of C in $$\ce{CH4}$$?

options.why: Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{CO3^{2-}}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: A compound (ethane) is 79.9% C, 20.1% H by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.
That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to CH3; the molecular formula is C2H6.

questions.stem: A solid melts at 1,710 °C, is very hard and does not conduct electricity. It is most likely:

options.why: Molecular solids melt at low temperatures.

options.text: An ionic solid that conducts as a solid
options.why: Ionic solids do not conduct as solids.

questions.stem: A reaction has ΔH° = -67 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -49 J/(mol·K). Below what temperature is it thermodynamically favorable?

options.why: Correct. Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (with ΔH in J).
Convert ΔH to J (or ΔS to kJ).

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 1.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×1, so order 0 in B.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is 11 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = -4.44; K = 0.0118. Positive ΔG°: K less than 1.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O}$$, 38 g of $$\ce{CH4}$$ reacts with 67 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{CO2}$$ can form?

options.why: Not all of both reactants reacts.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Correct. O2 is the limiting reactant.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.019 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 170 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature falls by 8.1 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 5760 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
Divide by the moles of reactant.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1.8 M and [I₂] = 0.9 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.4 M. What is K?
Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -369 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -210 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and adding reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 482, 897, 6279, 11616 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 2 electrons, so it has 2 valence electrons.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Mg/$$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and Pb/$$\ce{Pb^{2+}}$$ half-cells. Which electrode is the anode?

options.text: Pb, where reduction occurs at the anode
options.why: Reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode.
The higher potential is reduced at the cathode.
Correct. The half-reaction with the lower reduction potential runs as oxidation at the anode.

questions.explanation: Mg (E° -2.37 V) is oxidized at the anode; Pb is reduced at the cathode.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.13 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 9.25) and 0.4 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.02 mol of HCl is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.
Correct. First react: H⁺ converts A⁻ to HA. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 3.75) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 90 mL. What is the pH after 45 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O(l)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.
Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.2 M solution of hypochlorous acid (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-8})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 1.948 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in 1/[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: 2X → X₂. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Mg²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.1 M I⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Would lowering the pH significantly change the solubility? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: No: I⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so H⁺ does not remove it.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of O.
Explain why the 1s peak of O has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of N.

rubric.criterion: O has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: O has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: N: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
